variants.headline: Party names a new leader
variants.sub: Leadership of a political party has changed in the colony.
variants.body:
A party has a new leader in {colony}. A change at the head of an organisation is a political fact; a change in its programme is a separate question. Readers considering {target} should not have to accept the second as a necessary consequence of the first.

We welcome {target} in this assessment. New leadership deserves the opportunity for a fair hearing, and recognition of that opportunity need not depend on inventing achievements before they occur.

variants.headline: Leadership changes hands
variants.sub: A new leader is now at the head of a party in {colony}.
variants.body:
The name at the head of a party has changed. The event invites attention to what leadership means, beyond the identity of the person holding it. In assessing {target}, the useful question concerns responsibility for a political organisation rather than an invented personal history.

We welcome {target} in this assessment. New leadership deserves the opportunity for a fair hearing, and recognition of that opportunity need not depend on inventing achievements before they occur.

variants.headline: A new name at the head of the party
variants.sub: A party has a new leader in {colony}.
variants.body:
New leadership gives a party a different person to answer for its public direction. That is the established development in {colony}. Any assessment of {target} should leave unreported policies, internal vote totals and explanations for the change outside the factual account of the event.

We welcome {target} in this assessment. New leadership deserves the opportunity for a fair hearing, and recognition of that opportunity need not depend on inventing achievements before they occur.
